difficultyReason: Single causal claim with one obvious confounder. The stimulus jumps from a correlation (new medication, fewer headaches) to a causal conclusion, and the correct answer supplies an alternative cause that arose at the same time. Matches the 1★ anchor: one clear weakener, one opposite-direction strengthener, and three distractors that are irrelevant, too narrow, or shift the subject.
stimulus: Dr. Halvorsen: Six weeks after I started prescribing a new migraine medication to my regular patients, the number of headache complaints they reported at follow-up visits had fallen by nearly a third. The medication is therefore responsible for the decline in their headaches.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens Dr. Halvorsen's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same six-week period, the clinic replaced the fluorescent lighting in its waiting area with fixtures that many patients had previously said triggered their headaches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who received the new medication reported fewer side effects than patients who had received the previously prescribed medication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Halvorsen has been treating migraine patients for more than twenty years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new medication is more expensive than the medication it replaced at Dr. Halvorsen's clinic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients at a neighboring clinic who were not prescribed the new medication also reported a drop in tension headaches during the same period.

explanations.correct: If the trigger lighting was removed during the very same period the medication was introduced, there is a plausible alternative cause for the drop in headache complaints. That alternative explanation directly undercuts the doctor's leap from correlation to causation.
explanations.A: Correct. Supplies an obvious confounding cause that operated over the same six weeks.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — patients who tolerate a medication better are likelier to take it, making the medication a more credible cause of the decline.
explanations.C: Irrelevant. The doctor's experience says nothing about whether this particular medication caused this particular drop.
explanations.D: Cost is accurate-but-irrelevant: it has no bearing on whether the medication reduces headaches.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The doctor's conclusion is about her migraine patients; a drop in tension headaches at another clinic is a neighboring claim, not the argument itself.

difficultyReason: Direct 1★ pattern: a single causal claim about an ethics policy. The correct answer denies the premise's load-bearing fact by showing the reported decrease reflects reporting behavior rather than actual conduct. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope comparison, and a subject-shift.
stimulus: Ethics officer: Last year our firm replaced its annual ethics workshop with a monthly online refresher course. In the twelve months that followed, the number of internal complaints about employee misconduct fell by half. Clearly, the monthly refresher is a more effective deterrent to misconduct than the annual workshop was.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ethics officer's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shortly before the monthly course was introduced, the firm quietly eliminated the anonymous hotline that employees had previously used to file most of their misconduct complaints.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The monthly refresher course takes, in total, less of each employee's time than the annual workshop did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Employees at a competing firm that also uses monthly refresher courses report high satisfaction with them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the complaints filed in previous years concerned conduct by senior managers rather than by junior employees.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The monthly refresher course includes a short quiz that employees had generally rated as useful.

explanations.correct: If the main reporting channel was removed, a drop in recorded complaints tells us little about actual misconduct. The argument's premise — that fewer complaints mean less misconduct — is no longer reliable, so the causal conclusion loses its footing.
explanations.A: Correct. Undermines the load-bearing premise that complaint counts reflect misconduct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. Total time says nothing about deterrent effectiveness.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Satisfaction at another firm doesn't bear on whether the new course deters misconduct here.
explanations.D: Describes who filed past complaints; doesn't address the move from complaint counts to misconduct levels.
explanations.E: Strengthens, if anything — a useful quiz is some evidence the course is engaging.

difficultyReason: Textbook 1★: a single causal leap from a price change to a sales change, with a clear confounder (competitor closure) available. Traps include the strengthener, an unwarranted comparison, and an accurate-but-irrelevant fact about pricing policy.
stimulus: Store owner: In March, we dropped the price of our store-brand coffee by fifteen percent. Over the following two months, sales of that coffee rose by more than twenty percent compared with the two months before the price cut. The price reduction must be what drove the additional sales.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the store owner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store-brand tea, whose price was not reduced, sold slightly fewer units over the same period than in the preceding two months.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A competing grocery chain closed its two nearest locations at the beginning of March, and customers from those stores began shopping at the owner's store.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The store's national-brand coffee is still more expensive, per ounce, than its store-brand coffee.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Customers who bought the store-brand coffee said, in surveys, that they appreciated the lower price.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The store owner has reduced prices on several other products in the past year.

explanations.correct: The arrival of customers displaced from closed competitor stores is an obvious alternative cause of the sales increase that operated over the same period. With that confounder in play, the price cut no longer has to do the explaining.
explanations.A: A neighboring data point; doesn't address whether the price cut, rather than something else, drove coffee sales.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces an independent cause of the increase.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — the argument isn't about the national brand.
explanations.D: Strengthens, if anything — customer appreciation of the lower price supports the owner's causal story.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The owner's pricing history doesn't speak to this particular cause.

difficultyReason: Generalizing-from-a-sample stimulus at the 1★ level: a public defender concludes a program reduces reoffending, and the correct answer reveals a selection effect that makes the sample unrepresentative. Distractors include an opposite-direction strengthener and two irrelevancies.
stimulus: Public defender: Of the defendants whom our county routed through the new restorative-justice program last year, only ten percent were arrested again within six months. Among defendants in similar cases who went through standard sentencing, the six-month rearrest rate was almost thirty percent. These figures show that the restorative-justice program is substantially better than standard sentencing at preventing reoffending.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the public defender's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judges referred defendants to the restorative-justice program only if the prosecutor, the defense, and the victim all agreed the defendant was unlikely to reoffend.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Standard sentencing in the county typically involves a fine, probation, or a short jail term.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The restorative-justice program has been used in several neighboring counties for more than a decade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defendants who completed the restorative-justice program reported that they felt better understood by the court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A defendant's six-month rearrest rate is one of the most commonly cited measures of reoffending.

explanations.correct: If only defendants already judged unlikely to reoffend were admitted to the program, the low rearrest rate reflects who was picked, not what the program did. The comparison with standard-sentencing defendants is no longer apples-to-apples, which undermines the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a selection effect that supplies an alternative explanation for the lower rearrest rate.
explanations.B: Background about the comparison group; doesn't threaten the causal inference.
explanations.C: History of use elsewhere is accurate but irrelevant.
explanations.D: Strengthens, if anything — a sense of being understood is often linked to compliance.
explanations.E: Endorses the metric; doesn't weaken the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Simple 1★ causal argument in environmental science: a single causal claim (cleanup caused fish recovery) paired with an available confounder (a stocking program). Wrong answers include a strengthener and two accurate-but-irrelevant facts.
stimulus: Park ranger: Since our team finished removing the old tire dump from the banks of Miller Creek three years ago, the creek's native trout population has nearly doubled. The removal of the dump is clearly what allowed the trout to rebound.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the park ranger's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the same year the dump was removed, the state began releasing thousands of young native trout into Miller Creek every spring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Samples taken before the cleanup showed that leachate from the tire dump contained compounds toxic to aquatic life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Miller Creek is popular with recreational anglers, several of whom have praised the cleanup.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tires removed from the dump were recycled rather than sent to a landfill.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Native trout have also rebounded in a nearby creek that has never had a tire dump nearby.

explanations.correct: A hatchery-stocking program begun at the same time supplies an independent cause of the population increase. The cleanup no longer needs to be the reason, so the ranger's causal conclusion is undercut.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides an alternative cause that coincides with the cleanup.
explanations.B: Strengthens — it reinforces the premise that the dump was harming the fish.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Praise from anglers doesn't address the fish population's cause.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. What happened to the tires after removal doesn't bear on the trout.
explanations.E: Shift in subject; reports a neighboring trend rather than challenging this creek's causal story.

difficultyReason: 1★ causal argument in technology: the IT manager attributes reduced help-desk tickets to a new training video. The correct answer supplies a competing cause (a simultaneous software update) that operated over the same window. Wrong answers include a strengthener and two accurate-but-irrelevant facts.
stimulus: IT manager: After we required all employees to watch a short training video on the new email system, the number of help-desk tickets about email problems dropped by forty percent in the following month. The training video must be responsible for the drop.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the IT manager's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same month, the vendor pushed an automatic update that fixed several of the bugs that had generated most of the previous month's email tickets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Employees rated the training video as clearer than the written instructions they had previously been given.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The training video is longer than most other training videos the company has produced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Help-desk tickets about unrelated software have remained at roughly their usual level for several months.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few employees in another department had already watched an earlier version of the training video.

explanations.correct: If the vendor fixed the very bugs driving most of last month's tickets, the ticket drop has a plausible alternative cause. The training video no longer has to explain the change, so the causal conclusion is weakened.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides a competing cause that operated in the same month.
explanations.B: Strengthens — perceived clarity is evidence the video could help.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Video length doesn't bear on effectiveness here.
explanations.D: Steady levels elsewhere don't challenge the causal story for email tickets.
explanations.E: Too narrow — a small early-exposure group doesn't explain a forty-percent drop.

difficultyReason: 1★ causal argument in linguistics: a teacher concludes a new drill caused higher exam scores. The correct answer presents a clean confounder (an easier exam form). Distractors include a strengthener and a subject-shift.
stimulus: Language teacher: This semester I replaced our weekly vocabulary quiz with a short speaking drill on Fridays. My students' average score on the end-of-semester exam rose by twelve points compared with last semester's class. The speaking drill was clearly what produced the higher exam scores.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the language teacher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This semester's end-of-semester exam used a different form that the department's testing office had previously rated as substantially easier than last semester's form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students this semester said they enjoyed the speaking drill more than last semester's students had enjoyed the vocabulary quiz.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The speaking drill covered vocabulary in addition to pronunciation and grammar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students in a different section of the course, who did not do the speaking drill, scored about the same this semester as last semester.

choices.label: E
choices.text: End-of-semester exam scores in the teacher's other courses have stayed roughly constant for several years.

explanations.correct: If this semester's exam was simply easier, higher average scores would be expected no matter what happened in class. That undermines the leap from the score increase to the drill as cause.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides an alternative explanation for the higher scores.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — enjoyment tends to support engagement with the drill.
explanations.C: Too narrow — coverage overlap doesn't by itself explain the twelve-point jump.
explanations.D: Neighboring claim. Relevant to the drill's effectiveness in that other section, not to the teacher's causal inference.
explanations.E: Background about unrelated courses; doesn't challenge this semester's inference.

difficultyReason: 1★ analogical argument in history: a journalist generalizes from past campaigns to conclude a current one will succeed. The correct answer shows the analogy fails on the load-bearing feature. Distractors include a strengthener and irrelevancies.
stimulus: Journalist: Every successful pamphlet campaign in this country's history began with a vivid, emotionally charged image on the front page. The new public-health pamphlet launched last week also features a vivid, emotionally charged image on the front page. We can therefore expect it to succeed as well.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the journalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unlike earlier successful pamphlet campaigns, the new campaign is being distributed almost entirely through the mail rather than handed out in crowded public spaces.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The image on the new pamphlet was designed by an illustrator whose earlier work has received several awards.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earlier successful pamphlet campaigns addressed topics such as sanitation and voting, not public health.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The public-health pamphlet is printed on heavier paper than earlier pamphlets were.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The journalist has studied pamphlet campaigns for many years.

explanations.correct: If the earlier campaigns succeeded only when handed out in crowds, and the new one lacks that distribution channel, the analogy breaks on a plausibly load-bearing feature. The prediction of similar success is no longer well-supported.
explanations.A: Correct. Breaks the analogy by showing a relevant difference.
explanations.B: Strengthens — a skilled illustrator supports the prediction.
explanations.C: Topic difference, but the journalist's generalization was about the image, not the topic.
explanations.D: Paper weight is accurate but irrelevant.
explanations.E: The journalist's expertise is irrelevant to whether the analogy holds.

difficultyReason: 1★ predictive argument in policy: a city council member predicts a library-hours extension will drive a particular metric, and the correct answer offers a confounding cause for the premise. Distractors include a strengthener and a subject-shift.
stimulus: Council member: Three months ago the city library extended its weekday hours until nine in the evening. Since then, recorded library attendance on weekday evenings has risen by about a quarter. If we extend the hours at the community recreation center in the same way, its evening attendance will rise as well.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the same time the library extended its hours, a large office building opened across the street, bringing hundreds of workers into the area each evening.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The community recreation center is already open until eight in the evening.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Library staff report that evening patrons ask for help finding books slightly more often than daytime patrons do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A survey found that library patrons value the option of visiting in the evening.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weekday afternoon attendance at the library has remained roughly constant since the hours were extended.

explanations.correct: If a new office opened at the same time, the evening-attendance jump at the library likely reflects those new workers rather than the extended hours. Without the evidence that hours caused the jump, the prediction for the recreation center is undercut.
explanations.A: Correct. Alternative cause removes the support for the generalization.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. The argument is about extending hours, not current closing time.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — it describes staff interactions, not why attendance rose.
explanations.D: Strengthens — patrons valuing evenings supports the causal story.
explanations.E: Neutral background; doesn't threaten the evening-hours inference.

difficultyReason: 1★ causal argument in the arts: a gallery director attributes a ticket-sales spike to a new lighting design. The correct answer supplies a clear confounder (a feature review of the exhibit in a widely read paper) operating over the same window. Distractors include a strengthener and two accurate-but-irrelevant details.
stimulus: Gallery director: When we reinstalled our landscape exhibit last month, we replaced the overhead spotlights with softer, side-mounted lighting. In the four weeks since, ticket sales for that exhibit have climbed by nearly thirty percent compared with the previous four weeks. The new lighting must be drawing the extra visitors.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the gallery director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A widely read weekend newspaper published a glowing feature on the landscape exhibit the same week the new lighting was installed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Visitors who returned to the exhibit after the reinstall said they noticed the different lighting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gallery's other exhibits use the same overhead spotlights that were replaced in the landscape hall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new lighting fixtures cost slightly more to run than the fixtures they replaced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attendance at the gallery's gift shop has risen only modestly over the same four-week period.

explanations.correct: A glowing feature in a widely read paper is a classic alternative cause of a sudden attendance spike. Once that cause is on the table, the lighting change no longer has to do the explaining.
explanations.A: Correct. Supplies an independent cause for the sales increase.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — noticing the change is consistent with its drawing visitors.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Lighting elsewhere doesn't bear on this exhibit.
explanations.D: Operating cost is accurate but irrelevant to attendance.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Gift-shop traffic is a neighboring measure and doesn't undercut the lighting claim.
